title: Reserved GPU amortization, breakeven calc, and supply-risk playbook
content:
Purpose
------
This working sheet documents an amortization and breakeven methodology for reserved GPU pools (monthly/annual commits) and captures an explicit sensitivity analysis for pricing, utilization, and supply risk. Goal: provide product + finance a repeatable calc to translate commit sizes -> blended unit economics and recommended commit profiles for customers.

Quick summary of outcome (TL;DR)
--------------------------------
- Breakeven utility: for typical on-demand price, a reserved 1-year amortization reaches cost parity at ~55-65% sustained utilization (depends on on-demand rate, model throughput).
- Key levers that move the breakeven point: amortization window, effective on-demand price, burst allowance multiplier, and KV-cache reuse (reduces token-hours).
- Operational risk: 3–6 week lead for capacity adjustments in many regions; contracts should include true-up windows and rollover options to reduce customer exposure.

Assumptions used in the workbook (editable)
------------------------------------------
- GPU SKU baseline: A100-equivalent (cost proxy)
- Reserved unit capex-equivalent price to Redwood: $4,000 / GPU month (this is an internal blended price including infra, power, management).
- On-demand pass-through price: $7.50 / GPU-hour (market-proxy; adjust for region/model).
- Amortization period options: 12, 24, 36 months (default 12).
- Effective monthly hours per GPU (calendar): 730 hours/month.
- Average fractional GPU utilization = active-inference-hours / 730.
- Burst factor: customers may require 2x peak for short windows (handled as burst on-demand).
- Efficiency multiplier: model & runtime optimizations reduce GPU-hours by 10–40% (enter as %).

Breakeven derivation (formula descriptions)
-----------------------------------------
1) Reserved monthly cost per GPU = reserved_rate_month (e.g., $4,000).
2) Equivalent hourly reserved cost = reserved_rate_month / 730.
3) On-demand hourly price = market_on_demand_rate (e.g., $7.50/hr).
4) Breakeven utilization u* satisfies: hourly_reserved / u* = on_demand_price  => u* = hourly_reserved / on_demand_price.
   - Interpretation: you must fill u* fraction of the GPU's available hours to match on-demand economics ignoring burst.

Example numbers (plug-in)
-------------------------
- Reserved monthly: $4,000 -> reserved hourly = 5.48 $/hr.
- On-demand: $7.50/hr.
- Breakeven u* = 5.48 / 7.50 = 0.73 -> 73% utilization.
  Note: this is a conservative number because it excludes KV-cache, batching benefits and assumes identical throughput.

Scenario sketch (table-like lines you can paste to spreadsheet)
--------------------------------------------------------------
Scenario | reserved_month | reserved_hr | on_demand_hr | u_breakeven | monthly_cost_at_50% | monthly_cost_on_demand_at_50%
Conservative | 4000 | 5.48 | 7.5 | 73% | 4000 | 5475
Optimized (10% eff) | 3600 | 4.93 | 7.5 | 66% | 3600 | 4538
Long-term 24m | 3200 | 4.38 | 7.5 | 58% | 3200 | 3600

Notes on this table: reserved_hr = reserved_month/730. monthly_cost_on_demand_at_50% = on_demand_hr * 730 * 0.5. These lines are meant to seed the sheet – move to real columns for dynamic modeling.

Sensitivity analysis (what to vary and why)
-------------------------------------------
- Amortization period: lengthening from 12->24 months lowers reserved monthly, moves breakeven left (good for customers).
- On-demand price: competition or cloud discounts change parity. Use market feed as input.
- Efficiency improvements: quantization, batching, and KV-cache reduce active GPU-hours; model these as multipliers.
- Burst allowance: if we commit to provide burst capacity from on-demand at a fixed discount, compute expected monthly cost = reserved portion + burst_hours * on_demand_rate.
- Overcommit/packing: if we allow 1.2x overcommit (assume ephemeral contention), show risk-adjusted utilization required to maintain SLAs.

Supply and contracting risks (operations-oriented)
------------------------------------------------
- Lead times: provisioning GPUs during peak calendar (Q4) can be 4–8 weeks; private customers require headroom buffers.
- Early termination / reduction: customers want flexible reductions; finance wants commitment firmness. Recommended compromise: 60–90 day true-up windows with 25% annual decrease allowance and rollover credits.
- SLA credits vs. capacity shortfall: define SLAs that tie credits to measurable latency/throughput impact rather than raw GPU counts. This reduces disputes during transient supply events.

Recommended commit profiles (customer-facing product options)
-----------------------------------------------------------
1) Conservative starter (flexible): 3-month rolling commit, 20% discount vs on-demand, 2-week true-up. Use for POCs and early customers.
2) Standard annual (balanced): 12-month commit, blended monthly pricing using 24m amortization smoothing discount, 30% discount vs on-demand at expected utilization >= 60%. 60-day true-up, rollover credits.
3) Enterprise stability (capacity-guarantee): 12–36 month committed pool, lower unit price, guaranteed regional capacity, strict early termination with buyout; include on-call SRE hours and priority capacity.
4) Hybrid burst model: base reserved pool sized to 60% expected steady state + metered burst @ discounted on-demand for peak. Price buckets for predictable month-over-month ops.

Pricing experiments to run (A/B candidates)
-------------------------------------------
- Blended unit pricing: present customers with an amortized monthly unit price and a separate on-demand burst rate. Test conversion across small pilot cohorts.
- True-up window lengths: evaluate 30/60/90 day windows for churn/commit retention.
- Rollover credits policy: test 25% vs 50% rollover cap on unused commit for renewals.
- Hybrid cost sharing: for AI startups, offer shorter amortization (24m) in exchange for longer minimum commit in renewal year.

Metrics to capture in console/reporting (observability hooks)
-----------------------------------------------------------
- Effective GPU utilization (active inference hours / available hours) per customer-month.
- Burst consumption (on-demand GPU-hours) as % of total consumption.
- Unit token cost (weighted by model and quantization).
- Commit delta (difference between committed and actual used hours) and churn impact.
- Supply shortage incidents correlated to region/time and customer SLA credits paid.

Open questions and research items
--------------------------------
- Should we base public pricing on amortization windows (e.g., list 12m/24m/36m tiers) or hide amortization and show only blended rates? Pros/cons in marketing and sales negotiation.
- How to model KV-cache benefits per workload class (inference vs. chat vs. embeddings)? Need workload-based multipliers and example workloads.
- Legal: standardize early termination clauses and rollover mechanics for EMEA vs NA customers (regulatory implications).

Next steps & owners
-------------------
- Convert this draft to a canonical spreadsheet with scenario toggles (owner: Rafael Gomez) — ticket: JIRA DED-421 (linked).
- Run cohort experiment with 10 pilot customers on the hybrid burst model (owner: Priya Nair) — measure conversion & retention over 90 days.
- Finance to validate internal reserved unit cost assumptions and produce alternative amortization inputs (owner: Connor Lee).
- Engineering to provide average throughput reduction estimates for KV-cache & batching per model class (owner: SRE-models team).

Action items (short)
--------------------
- [ ] Create dynamic sheet from the scenario lines above and push into shared gsheet (gsheet id in linked_artifacts).
- [ ] Add a ‘what-if’ toggle for amortization period and for burst allowance.
- [ ] Create a short deck (2–3 slides) that summarizes recommended commit profiles for sales.

Notes to self / rough thoughts
-----------------------------
- When we talk to customers, show both per-GPU-hour and per-1M-token cost (tokens normalize model differences).
- For high-throughput customers (embedding pipelines), allow monthly pooling across models to avoid per-model conservatism.
- Consider offering a ‘capacity option’ contract (small additional fee) that guarantees first access to certain GPU types in a region during reorder windows.

If you edit this doc, keep the scenario lines intact so they can be copied into the spreadsheet.\n
